newsitem.title: MALTA: New Maltese premier tackles dockyard losses.
newsitem.headline: New Maltese premier tackles dockyard losses.

text.p: Self-management by the workers at Malta's loss-making dockyard is set to end.

New Maltese Prime Minister Alfred Sant surprised supporters and opponents last Friday by announcing that the managing council of the state-owned dockyard would be given a majority of government-appointed representatives following legislative changes to be rushed through parliament in a special sitting next Saturday.

The powerful General Workers' Union (GWU), which in 1994 blocked attempts by the former Nationalist government to be represented on the council, even as government subsidies to the yard increased, said on Monday that it understood change was necessary in the current circumstances.
Management by the workers was introduced by Labour prime minister Dom Mintoff in 1975 with the council members directly elected by the 3,500 workforce.

Malta University lecturer Godfrey Baldacchino, appointed by the new government two months ago to assess the dockyard, said in his report: "The workers and their representatives have taken over control of all decision-making, with the government and the yard's own management having no say in its policies."
Baldacchino's report followed another highly critical report, also commissioned by the government, into the dockyard's finances.
Accountant John Cassar White said the dockyard made a loss of 12.5 million pounds ($35 million) in 1996 after a similar loss in 1995. Accumulated losses had reached 70 million pounds.
Cassar White complained of poor financial controls and said the dockyard had been reduced to signing uneconomical ship-repair contracts.

That report lead to the setting up of a task force of representatives of the government, the GWU, the dockyard council and the dockyard's professional management to draw up a strategy for the yard. The task force recommended changing the council's composition, even though the council members argued against.

Sant told dockyard workers on Monday that the government could not continue to pump 15 million pounds into the yard every year, especially when that money could be used for building schools, which were a government priority.

The task force called for the recruitment of trained managers, including foreigners, and the strengthening of the dockyard's commercial and sales section for more aggressive marketing and public relations.
Malta Drydocks is among the oldest ship repair yards in the Mediterranean, linked with Malta's history as a naval base.

The British forces built five of its seven docks to serve the needs of the Royal Navy, but the dockyard came under Maltese ownership in the late sixties and its biggest dock, able to take supertankers of up to 350,000 tonnes, was built with Chinese financial and technical help in the mid-seventies.

At the height of the cold war the dockyard was banned from repairing American and Russian ships and it has since specialised on tankers, bulk carriers and cruise liners, with Britain's Cunard and P&0 among its most regular clients. Last summer Malta Drydocks beat off competition to repair Cunard's Royal Viking Sun after it ran aground off Port Said.
The dockyard, like other neighbouring yards, started making losses in the early eighties, with its survival increasingly depandent on hand-outs from the government.
